title: Transfer pricing: how companies explain prices inside a group
audience: A curious adult arriving from another field. No background in tax, accounting, law, or business software is assumed.
scope: An introduction to cross-border transfer pricing and the people, records, and software behind its annual documentation cycle. It uses the common framework of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), with an EU example in the history. Countries set their own legal requirements; OECD guidance is not a worldwide filing law. Detailed tax calculations, customs duties, and country-specific filing instructions are outside this guide. Luma, its people, countries A and B, and all amounts are fictional teaching examples.
learningGoals: Explain why a price between two companies in one group matters for tax.
Connect a price explanation to the work, resources, and risks of each company.
Distinguish the main documentation packages and follow a complete preparation cycle.
Explain where software helps and why consistent documents still need human review.

introduction.whatItIs: Imagine a lamp made in one country and sold in another. The factory and the local seller belong to the same business group, but they are separate companies. The factory charges the seller for the lamp. That internal charge is a transfer price. Similar charges arise when related companies provide services, lend money, or let each other use a brand or invention.
introduction.whyItMatters: A higher purchase price leaves less profit with the seller and more with the factory. Tax authorities therefore want to understand how the group chose its terms. Transfer pricing compliance means applying the relevant rules and keeping a supportable explanation of what happened. A compliance platform helps people collect facts, review calculations, prepare reports, and track obligations.
introduction.familiarComparison: Think of two separately run stalls at a fair: one bakes cakes and another sells them. The price between the stalls affects how much each earns, even though the customer sees only the final price.
introduction.whereComparisonBreaks: Independent stall owners can bargain for themselves. Companies with common owners may follow a group decision instead. Separate countries also apply their own tax rules. A shared owner does not make the companies' separate tax responsibilities disappear.

participants.name: Business and local finance teams
participants.role: Run the factory or selling company and record sales, expenses, and internal charges. They know what actually happened.
participants.caresAbout: Accurate accounts, manageable requests, and descriptions that reflect their work. In our example, Leo manages the selling company's finances.

participants.name: The group's tax team
participants.role: Coordinates the explanation across companies, obtains expert review, and plans the reporting work. Sofia leads this work at fictional Luma.
participants.caresAbout: Tax treatment the group can explain, deadlines, and consistency across countries. The group funds the software and any outside help.

participants.name: Legal colleagues and company decision-makers
participants.role: Maintain company and contract records and approve decisions within their responsibilities.
participants.caresAbout: Agreements that reflect real arrangements and a clear record of who authorized changes.

participants.name: Tax advisers and platform providers
participants.role: Supply specialist analysis, software, or document preparation. One provider may offer both software and services.
participants.caresAbout: Clear scope, reliable inputs, review time, and fees that cover the work. Outsourcing preparation still leaves the company with responsibilities.

participants.name: Tax authorities
participants.role: Administer local tax rules, assess risk, and examine selected cases. Each country's authority has its own role.
participants.caresAbout: Correct taxable profit and useful explanations. Receiving a report does not mean accepting every position in it.

participantsOverview.illustrationPrompt: Create a simple adult learning relationship map, not an organization chart or a money-flow diagram. Center: a woman coordinating documents, labeled 'Tax team'. Four surrounding separate illustrated cards: 'Business and finance' with a lamp factory and ledger; 'Legal team' with a contract; 'Advisers and platform' with a person and laptop; 'Tax authorities' with two separate office buildings. Four clear single-headed arrows only: Business and finance TO Tax team labeled 'Facts'; Legal team TO Tax team labeled 'Agreements'; Advisers and platform TO Tax team labeled 'Analysis and tools'; Tax team TO Tax authorities labeled 'Required reports'. No arrows between any other nodes, no government approval ticks, no currency, no flags, no corporate ownership lines. White space, navy and teal with restrained amber. Exactly these nine short labels, no other text. The relationships show contributions to preparation, not a complete legal filing map.

media.title: Who contributes to transfer pricing compliance
media.alt: Business and finance provide facts, legal colleagues provide agreements, and advisers and the platform provide analysis and tools to the tax team, which coordinates required reports for tax authorities.
media.caption: The tax team coordinates contributions. Each company still has its own responsibilities and applicable local requirements.

concepts.meaning: Related companies are connected through ownership or control; the precise legal test varies. A transfer price is the charge for something one supplies to another. Profit, in our simplified example, means sales income minus the included costs, before tax.
concepts.example: Luma's factory spends €60 making a lamp and charges its related seller €80. The seller sells it to a customer for €100 and incurs €10 of selling costs. Factory profit is €20; seller profit is €10. If the internal price were €90, those profits would become €30 and €0. Combined profit stays €30. This assumes the lamp is sold and ignores all other costs and taxes.
concepts.whyItMatters: Changing the internal price changes where profit appears without changing the customer's purchase. Neither illustrative price has been established as acceptable for tax.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Teach two alternative accounting cases using a very clean side-by-side comparison, not a time sequence. Two equal panels labeled 'Internal price €80' and 'Internal price €90'. Each panel has a small factory icon and a shop icon. In left panel labels under icons: 'Factory profit €20', 'Seller profit €10'. In right panel: 'Factory profit €30', 'Seller profit €0'. Along bottom of EACH panel one shared bar labeled 'Combined profit €30'. Bars must have identical total widths; left has factory two-thirds navy and seller one-third teal; right is fully navy. No arrows between panels, no coins multiplying, no tax rates, no claim either price is correct. Small shared footer: 'Illustrative, before tax'. Exactly the specified labels, very large type and abundant white space.

media.title: Related companies and transfer prices
media.alt: With an €80 internal price, factory and seller profits are €20 and €10. With a €90 price, they are €30 and €0. Both bars total €30.
media.caption: Two alternative cases with the same €100 customer sale and €70 combined costs. The internal price changes where the €30 profit appears; neither price is established as appropriate for tax.

concepts.meaning: Ask what independent businesses would have agreed in comparable circumstances. 'Arm's length' describes independence, not physical distance. The question includes payment terms and responsibilities as well as the price.
concepts.example: An unrelated seller buying one lamp for immediate payment may be a poor comparison for Luma's seller buying thousands, storing stock, and paying later.
concepts.whyItMatters: The test is neither 'whatever the group prefers' nor automatically the retail price. A sound analysis may support a range of results rather than one uniquely correct number.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Create two equal separate panels. Left heading 'Related companies': a factory and lamp shop inside one shared rounded boundary. Right heading 'Independent businesses': a factory and lamp shop each inside its own separate rounded boundary, with two people shaking hands between them. Under BOTH panels one large question 'Comparable circumstances?' and three icons labeled 'Quantity', 'Payment terms', 'Responsibilities'. Use ONLY these six text labels. Important: leave the space between panels completely empty. There must be NO equals sign anywhere, no comparison symbol, no balance scale, no magnifying glass, no connecting arrows between the two cases, no tax approval marks, no numbers. The illustration asks whether circumstances are comparable; it does not assert that the cases or prices are equal. Minimal adult editorial navy teal amber on warm white, very large labels.

media.title: The arm's length principle
media.alt: A factory and shop share one group boundary on the left; independent businesses have separate boundaries on the right. Quantity, payment terms, and responsibilities are compared.
media.caption: Compare the circumstances as well as the prices. An independent transaction is useful only when the relevant conditions are sufficiently comparable.

concepts.meaning: These three words organize a factual investigation, often called a functional analysis. Functions are the work people do; assets are resources they use, including equipment and valuable knowledge; risks are uncertainties that can bring gains or losses. Contracts matter alongside actual decisions, conduct, and the financial ability to bear a risk.
concepts.example: Who designs Luma's lamps? Who decides how much stock to hold? Who authorizes warranty repairs and bears their cost? A contract alone cannot answer whether daily practice follows that arrangement.
concepts.whyItMatters: Two companies called 'distributors' may do very different work. Their names or contract labels alone do not establish the profit each should earn.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Three equal, uncluttered teaching panels about a lamp business. Panel 'Functions' shows a person designing a lamp and another packing it. Panel 'Assets' shows workshop equipment and a lamp design drawing. Panel 'Risks' shows a manager considering unsold boxed lamps and a returned lamp needing repair; use a small question mark over the uncertain outcome. One bottom strip juxtaposes a signed contract and people actually working with label 'Check agreements against reality'. Exactly the three panel headings and bottom label only. No allocation percentages, no automatic profit arrows, no additional jargon or text.

media.title: Functions, assets, and risks
media.alt: Three panels show designing and packing lamps, equipment and designs, and uncertainty about stock and repairs. Below, a contract is checked against people doing the work.
media.caption: Describe the actual work, resources, and risks, and check how agreements relate to what people do.

concepts.meaning: Comparables are relevant observations about independent businesses or transactions. A pricing method is a structured way to use such information: for example, comparing transaction prices, adding an appropriate profit to costs, or examining profit relative to sales. That last relationship is a profit margin. Method choice depends on the facts and reliable information available.
concepts.example: Sofia checks whether other sellers perform similar work in similar markets. A business developing its own distinctive lamp designs may be unsuitable for comparison with a seller that only distributes lamps.
concepts.whyItMatters: A database supplies candidates, not an automatic answer. The team must explain its selection and important differences. There is no universal percentage to apply to every internal charge.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: A tax analyst at a clear desk compares three large illustrated candidate cards with Luma's simple lamp-selling shop. Candidate cards depict a comparable lamp shop, a factory, and a design studio. Analyst uses a magnifying glass to inspect them, not automatically approve one. Above cards label 'Possible comparisons'; below three short question labels 'Similar work?', 'Similar market?', 'Useful data?'. No price, numeric percentage, ranking, pass stamp, traffic light, or extra text. Leave results visibly under review. Adult minimal navy teal illustration with amber questions.

media.title: Comparables and pricing methods
media.alt: An analyst compares Luma’s lamp shop with candidate businesses: a lamp shop, a factory, and a design studio. Questions concern work, market, and useful data.
media.caption: Candidates need review. Similar products do not automatically mean similar responsibilities or useful comparison data.

concepts.meaning: A policy describes the intended approach to internal charges. Actual results are what the accounts record. Reconciliation means checking how records fit together and explaining differences. Some cases require an adjustment, but correcting a data error and changing a price are different actions.
concepts.example: One spreadsheet shows Luma's lamp purchase at €90 while the invoice and accounts show €80. Sofia first investigates the mismatch. Editing the invoice merely to match the spreadsheet would conceal the problem.
concepts.whyItMatters: A sensible policy can be implemented incorrectly. Before considering a pricing adjustment, the team needs reliable figures and a reason that fits the facts and applicable rules.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Three large documents side by side on a review desk. Left labeled 'Spreadsheet' prominently shows '€90'. Middle labeled 'Invoice' shows '€80'. Right labeled 'Accounts' shows '€80'. A person points to the mismatch using an amber magnifying glass. Bottom question 'Why the difference?' No arrows rewriting or changing numbers, no checks or approval marks, no assumption which source is correct, no other text. The lesson is investigation before changing records, not a recommended tax adjustment. Very clear typography, navy teal and amber on warm white.

media.title: Policy, actual results, and reconciliation
media.alt: A reviewer investigates a spreadsheet showing €90 beside an invoice and accounts each showing €80.
media.caption: Investigate the mismatch before deciding whether a record or a pricing decision needs to change.

concepts.term: Master file, local file, and country-by-country report
concepts.meaning: The OECD documentation framework contains three views. A master file explains the group as a whole. A local file examines relevant transactions of a local company, including the analysis and financial information. A country-by-country report summarizes information such as revenue, profit, tax, and activity by country for groups within its scope. It is often shortened to CbCR.
concepts.example: Think of a group portrait, a close-up of Luma's seller, and a country summary table. They answer different questions. Local law determines which documents are required, their contents, and whether they are filed routinely or kept ready for a request.
concepts.whyItMatters: CbCR helps authorities identify risks; it does not prove an individual price is right. Public country-by-country reporting, such as the EU regime, is a separate disclosure obligation with its own rules.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Three equally sized side-by-side document covers, not nested and not linked in a mandatory sequence. Cover 1 title 'Master file', subtitle 'Group overview', simple icon of several linked companies. Cover 2 title 'Local file', subtitle 'Local transactions', magnifying glass on one company and invoice. Cover 3 title 'Country-by-country report', subtitle 'Country summaries', simple abstract table with no real figures. Small shared footer 'Requirements depend on local rules'. Exactly these seven labels and no other text. Do not show every company filing all three, no public website globe, no confidential lock that implies all documents always confidential, no checkmarks.

media.title: Master file, local file, and country-by-country report
media.alt: Three document covers show a group overview, a local company and its transactions, and a table of country summaries.
media.caption: These views answer different questions. Local rules determine which documents are needed and how they are handled.

concepts.meaning: An audit trail connects a reported conclusion to its inputs, calculations, versions, and reviewers. Here, an audit means an examination by a tax authority. The trail helps someone reconstruct the work later; it does not guarantee the authority will agree.
concepts.example: For Luma's seller, Sofia can retrieve the source accounts, the comparison study, the explanation of a difference, and the approved version of the report.
concepts.whyItMatters: A polished document is much more useful when its statements can be checked. Software can preserve the chain, while people remain responsible for the reasoning and review.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: An extremely simple four-station diagram. All stations equal size, left to right. Label 1 'Source records': icon of three sheets with abstract horizontal lines. Label 2 'Analysis': icon of a blank grid and magnifying glass. Label 3 'Human review': person examining a sheet with abstract horizontal lines. Label 4 'Saved report': icon of layered folders. Three right-facing arrows connect these four stations. Under them a dotted return arrow runs from the last folder back to the first sheets, labeled 'Trace the explanation'. Exactly these FIVE labels and no other text anywhere. All papers show only abstract lines. No calculator, no numerals, no percentages, no amounts, no price, no markup, no dates, no formula, no extra labels inside stations, no approval stamps. It teaches record traceability, not any pricing method. Navy teal warm white with restrained amber; extremely large labels and uncluttered icons.

media.title: An audit trail
media.alt: Source records lead through analysis and human review to a saved report. A return arrow traces the explanation back to the source records.
media.caption: A reviewer should be able to work backward from the report to the supporting records, analysis, and review.

historyNote: These selected OECD and EU milestones explain today's shared vocabulary and reporting work. They are not a complete global history, and countries have followed different paths. The practical lessons are teaching interpretations.

history.change: The OECD's 1995 Transfer Pricing Guidelines built on its 1979 report on transfer pricing and multinational enterprises.
history.whyItMatters: International business needed ways to discuss internal prices across separate tax systems. Shared guidance provided a common reference without replacing national law.

history.change: The OECD/G20 project on Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) addressed ways businesses reduce or shift taxable profits. Its Action 13 report set out the master file, local file, and country-by-country reporting framework.
history.whyItMatters: The resulting reporting work connects local transactions with the wider group. Reusing consistent information across documents becomes valuable.

history.period: 2021: the EU adds a public reporting regime
history.change: The EU's public country-by-country reporting directive entered into force in December 2021, introducing disclosure requirements for businesses within its scope.
history.whyItMatters: Some information now has a wider audience than tax authorities. Teams must distinguish public reporting from tax-authority reporting, including their separate scope and timing.

walkthrough.title: Sofia prepares Luma's annual explanation
walkthrough.setup: Follow one fictional lamp transaction within a fictional multinational group. Luma Manufacturing in country A supplies Luma Sales in country B. Sofia coordinates tax work; Leo supplies the seller's facts and accounts. The €60 cost, €80 internal price, €100 customer price, and €10 selling cost illustrate arithmetic only, not a benchmark or recommended price.

steps.title: Map the work and the obligations
steps.whatHappens: Sofia identifies the companies, transaction, reporting year, and responsible people. With local specialists, she checks which reports and notifications apply, their deadlines, and whether they must be submitted or retained.
steps.whyItMatters: The team's task list comes from applicable requirements. Having a template does not make that document mandatory.

steps.title: Understand the business behind the contract
steps.whatHappens: Leo explains ordering, storage, sales, and repairs. Legal colleagues provide the agreement. Sofia records who performs the work and makes decisions, checking the description with the people involved.
steps.whyItMatters: The price analysis needs an accurate business story before it needs polished wording.

steps.title: Develop and explain the analysis
steps.whatHappens: Sofia and an adviser choose to examine seller profit relative to sales, recording why that method and the selected comparisons suit their assumed facts. Here €10 from €100 of sales is a 10% margin. Arithmetic alone does not establish whether that result is supportable.
steps.whyItMatters: A calculation can be correct even when the comparison or assumptions behind it are unsuitable.

steps.title: Check actual results and investigate a change
steps.whatHappens: Leo connects the transaction figures to the accounts and explains differences. He also reports that the seller began authorizing and paying for warranty repairs during the year, while the earlier description assigned those responsibilities to the factory.
steps.whyItMatters: Sofia reopens the business description and analysis with the adviser instead of copying the old conclusion.
steps.watchOut: The change may affect the analysis, but it does not by itself dictate a new price. The team checks the facts, timing, contracts, and relevant rules before deciding what to update.

steps.title: Prepare, localize, and review the documents
steps.whatHappens: The team updates the repair description and affected analysis, then the platform assembles drafts. Sofia checks shared statements, Leo checks numbers, and local specialists check content and language. Reviewers resolve open issues before approving final versions.
steps.whyItMatters: A generated draft saves assembly work. It still needs checks that the explanation is accurate and locally suitable.

steps.title: Complete the obligations and keep the trail
steps.whatHappens: The responsible people submit what is required through the relevant channels, keep confirmations, and retain other required records. Sofia archives the supporting work and records changes to revisit next year.
steps.whyItMatters: Completion includes evidence of submission where needed and the ability to answer later questions. An exported file alone proves neither.

walkthrough.outcome: Luma has a reviewed explanation, traceable figures, and a record of completed obligations. The repair change is addressed rather than hidden in reused text. This case does not establish an acceptable real-world price or predict a tax authority's decision.
walkthrough.illustrationPrompt: Six-panel adult teaching storyboard in a strict 3-column by 2-row grid, read left to right across top row then left to right across bottom row. Consistent characters: Sofia, woman with dark bob hair and teal jacket; Leo, man with short dark hair and amber sweater. Same simple desk lamp motif throughout. Panel 1 '1 Map': Sofia with two company cards and calendar. Panel 2 '2 Understand': Sofia interviewing Leo beside lamp stock and a contract. Panel 3 '3 Analyze': Sofia and adviser inspect comparison cards and calculator, no numbers. Panel 4 '4 Investigate change': Leo shows a broken lamp being repaired, Sofia revisits a folder, amber question mark, not disaster. Panel 5 '5 Review': both review a document at a laptop with another reviewer. Panel 6 '6 Submit and retain': report sent to a receiving tray plus separate archive folder, no authority approval. Exactly the six panel titles, no extra text, no percentages, no amounts, no flags, no progress arrows between panels, no courtroom or final victory stamp. Strong numbering and ample white space.

media.title: Sofia’s annual documentation cycle
media.alt: Six scenes follow Sofia and Leo as they map obligations, understand the business, analyze comparisons, investigate changed repair responsibilities, review documents, and submit and retain records.
media.caption: The repair change sends Sofia back to the business facts and analysis before the documents are finalized. Read the six scenes from left to right across each row.

valueAndIncentives.title: The group buys dependable preparation
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Software subscriptions and specialist fees pay for coordination, reusable information, and reviewed documents. Time saved matters most when it also reduces missed obligations, unexplained differences, and repeated requests.
valueAndIncentives.example: Recording Luma's agreed business description once can prevent several local reports from telling conflicting stories.

valueAndIncentives.title: The service still costs human attention
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Major effort goes into collecting reliable data, evaluating comparisons, maintaining country knowledge, translation, and review. Providers may charge for access, document preparation, or advisory work.
valueAndIncentives.example: A fixed preparation fee can make costs predictable, but unusual transactions still need an agreed scope and enough expert time.

valueAndIncentives.title: Participants judge success differently
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Local teams want fewer interruptions; group teams want consistent answers; authorities need usable information. Their priorities can conflict when deadlines approach.
valueAndIncentives.example: A dashboard showing every draft as complete may look reassuring while Leo's repair question remains unresolved. Counting files alone misses that problem.

challenges.title: Finding useful comparisons
challenges.whyHard: Independent businesses rarely match perfectly, especially when valuable designs, brands, or unusual responsibilities are involved.
challenges.tradeOff: Narrower selection can improve similarity while leaving less data to analyze.
challenges.example: Excluding every seller with a different product may leave Sofia with no useful observations.
challenges.commonApproach: Explain the economically important differences and use reliable adjustments where possible. Document uncertainty; a larger database cannot guarantee a close match.

challenges.title: Getting numbers and business descriptions to agree
challenges.whyHard: Accounts, contracts, and operational knowledge come from different people and may describe different periods.
challenges.tradeOff: Early drafting helps meet deadlines, but premature finalization can preserve stale assumptions.
challenges.example: Luma's accounts include repair costs while its reused description still says the factory handles repairs.
challenges.commonApproach: Assign owners to facts and figures, reconcile totals, and flag changes for review. A complete upload cannot confirm that people described the business correctly.

challenges.title: Sharing information while meeting local requirements
challenges.whyHard: Countries can differ in scope, content, language, deadlines, and submission rules. A shared framework does not remove these differences.
challenges.tradeOff: Common templates save effort; excessive uniformity can omit a local requirement.
challenges.example: Sofia may need to retain one country's document but actively submit another country's report.
challenges.commonApproach: Combine shared facts with reviewed local requirements and dated rule sources. Check changes before each cycle; translating a document alone does not make it locally suitable.

challenges.title: Resolving disagreement across countries
challenges.whyHard: One authority may increase a company's taxable profit without the other country immediately granting a corresponding reduction. The same profit can then be taxed twice.
challenges.tradeOff: Seeking certainty requires time and specialist resources, while unresolved disputes consume attention and cash.
challenges.example: Country A increases Luma Manufacturing's taxable profit; relief for Luma Sales in country B is a separate matter.
challenges.commonApproach: Preserve the supporting analysis and assess available remedies. A treaty's mutual agreement procedure lets authorities work to resolve disputes; an advance pricing arrangement can establish an approach for future covered transactions. Access, conditions, and outcomes depend on the case.

challenges.title: Automating work without hiding weak reasoning
challenges.whyHard: Software can reproduce an outdated assumption consistently across many files. Fluent AI text can make an unsupported explanation sound convincing.
challenges.tradeOff: More automation speeds assembly but increases the reach of an unnoticed error.
challenges.example: A drafting assistant repeats Luma's old repair arrangement in every translated report.
challenges.commonApproach: Keep source links, visible review status, and named reviewers for important claims. Restrict sensitive information to the people who need it. A technical validation pass checks only what its rules actually test.

misconceptions.reality: Related companies need terms for ordinary business transactions. Those terms can be misused, but the existence of an internal charge does not establish abuse.

misconceptions.belief: A signed contract proves the price is acceptable.
misconceptions.reality: It is part of the explanation. Actual conduct, relevant comparisons, and applicable rules still matter.

misconceptions.belief: Every company must file all three documentation packages.
misconceptions.reality: Requirements depend on the company, group, transaction, year, and local rules. The three packages are distinct views, not a universal filing checklist.

misconceptions.belief: A loss or a filed report settles the question.
misconceptions.reality: A loss can have ordinary business causes and deserves investigation. Filing establishes that something was submitted; it does not establish that its pricing analysis is correct.

takeaways: Internal prices affect where profit is recorded, so their explanation matters to more than one company and country.
Start with the real work and arrangements, then connect the method, figures, and documents.
Group, local, and country-summary views have different purposes and requirements.
A useful platform supports coordination and traceability; reviewed reasoning and completed obligations remain the goal.

knowledgeChecks.question: In the simplified lamp example, the internal price rises from €80 to €90. The final sale and other costs stay the same. What changes?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Factory profit rises from €20 to €30, while seller profit falls from €10 to €0. Combined profit remains €30.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The internal sale is income for one company and a cost for the other. This calculation says nothing about which price is acceptable for tax.

knowledgeChecks.question: The contract says the factory handles repairs, but Leo says the seller now decides and pays for them. Is updating the report's wording enough?
knowledgeChecks.answer: No. Check the changed responsibilities, their timing, and their effect on the analysis with the appropriate reviewers.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: A factual change can affect the comparison and conclusion. Better wording alone cannot resolve that question.

knowledgeChecks.question: A country-by-country summary totals correctly. Does that establish that Luma's lamp price is appropriate?
knowledgeChecks.answer: No. The summary helps identify risks; individual transactions still need their own supporting analysis.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: A correct total answers a different question from whether a price reflects comparable independent arrangements.

knowledgeChecks.question: The platform exports every final report. What must Sofia check before calling the cycle complete?
knowledgeChecks.answer: That required reviews are complete, applicable submissions and notifications are made, and supporting records and confirmations are retained.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Creating an output file is one step in fulfilling an obligation. Some documents are submitted; others must be kept available.

nextQuestions: Which transactions and business changes require the most judgment here?
